research_topic: Improve forgetting resistance in continual learning by developing task-ordering strategies for standard benchmarks using 1–3B parameter models with efficient adaptation, curriculum learning from task similarity and gradient interference, and rigorous evaluation with baselines, ablations, overhead analysis, transfer metrics, and full reproducibility.

new_method.method:
Open Problems: Task order strongly affects both forgetting and forward transfer in continual learning, yet current CL systems either use the natural data stream or simple heuristics (random, semantic similarity) to decide the next task.  For 1–3 B-parameter backbones this is critical because (a) replay or rehearsal budgets are tiny relative to the model, (b) full fine-tuning previews to estimate interference are prohibitively expensive, and (c) larger models amplify gradient interference.  The open problem is therefore: How can we choose – on-the-fly and with negligible extra compute – a curriculum (ordering and optional interleaving) that minimises worst-case forgetting while still maximising positive transfer for large-scale PEFT-based continual learners?
Methods: We propose CURIOUS (Compute-budgeted Utility-aware Reordering for Interference-Optimised Ultra-large Streams), an online task scheduler that couples (i) cheap surrogate metrics of future interference with (ii) a bandit-style meta-controller that selects the next task to train.

1. Surrogate metrics (computed once at task arrival)
   a. Data similarity score S_d: Optimal-Transport Dataset Distance (OTDD) between the new task minibatch and a 1 k-sample memory sketch of every previous task (fast GPU Sinkhorn).  
   b. Gradient conflict score S_g: For each previous task we keep a frozen 1-layer linear probe on top of the backbone.  A single PEFT (LoRA-r=4) forward-backward pass on 128 samples of the new task yields its gradient g_new; we store per-task reference gradients g_i (updated every N steps).  Cosine similarity gives conflict = −⟨g_new, g_i⟩.
   c. Stability estimate S_s: moving average of forgetting the model has suffered on task i so far (from continual-eval metrics such as min-ACC).
2. Utility function U(i,new) = α S_d + β S_g + γ S_s (α,β,γ learned online via REINFORCE on final ACC proxy).
3. Meta-controller: A non-stationary stochastic multi-armed bandit where each arm is one admissible permutation produced by a cheap beam search using U.  Reward is validation ACC drop after k mini-batches; arms are updated with Thompson Sampling.
4. Execution: CURIOUS proposes either (a) the next whole task to train or (b) an interleaving ratio (e.g. 70 % current + 30 % best-transfer old task) implemented via a Round-Robin dataloader.  All computations use the same PEFT adapters as training; no extra forward pass on the full model.
5. Overhead guardrail: Scheduler limited to <3 % additional FLOPs by capping sample sizes and sharing the PEFT gradients already produced for first optimiser step.
Experimental Setup: Backbones: LLaMA-2-1.3 B for NLP stream; ViT-Huge-14 (≈2 B params) for CV stream, both fine-tuned with LoRA (r=32) + classifier head.
Streams:
1. CTrL-Slong-100 (vision, 100 tasks, ResNet18 baseline in original paper) scaled to ViT images.
2. FLAN-Mix-20: 20 diverse NLP tasks (QA, reasoning, code) each 5 k samples.
3. CAT mixed similar/dissimilar sequence (10 tasks).
Baselines: Random order, chronological, similarity-only ordering (dOTDD), gradient-only ordering (GradNorm), and theoretical diverse-first order (from “Theory on Forgetting…”).
Metrics: ACC, BWT, FWT, min-ACC, WC-ACC, stability-gap (WF_10, WF_100), compute & memory overhead, energy (CodeCarbon).
Ablations: (i) remove S_g or S_d; (ii) bandit→greedy; (iii) different LoRA ranks; (iv) task arrival delay.
Robustness: repeat with 3 random seeds and with 30 % noisy labels injected into 25 % of tasks.
Result: We expect CURIOUS to
• increase final ACC by 3-5 % over best heuristic baseline and 7-10 % over random order on all three streams.
• halve average forgetting (BWT from −0.12 to −0.05 on CTrL-Slong) and reduce min-ACC drop by >30 %.
• Match or exceed forward transfer (FWT) of similarity-based ordering.
• Maintain overhead <3 % FLOPs, <1 % extra GPU memory.
• Ablations show β≈0.6 importance of gradient conflict; removing bandit reduces gains by ~40 %.
Conclusion: CURIOUS demonstrates that intelligent, compute-aware curriculum construction is feasible for billion-scale continual learners using only lightweight PEFT probes.  By unifying data similarity, gradient interference, and stability into a single utility-driven bandit, CURIOUS consistently mitigates forgetting without sacrificing transfer or efficiency.  Practically, it yields plug-and-play schedulers for real-time learning systems where task order is flexible (e.g., edge-deployed adaptive assistants).  Academically, it opens avenues for:
• theoretical analysis of utility-based curricula versus stability-gap; 
• extension to task-free online streams via sample-level routing; 
• integration with dynamic memory budgets and PEFT methods like HydraLoRA.  Future work can explore joint optimisation of memory replay selection and CURIOUS ordering, and port the scheduler to even larger models through parameter-sharing across probes.
